newsitem.title: USA: Three US Senators call for 15 pct flat tax in D.C..
newsitem.headline: Three US Senators call for 15 pct flat tax in D.C..

text.p: Three U.S. senators introduced legislation to establish a 15-percent flat tax in the financially pressed District of Columbia.

"This plan will jump start the District's economy and set in motion a commercial, cultural and social renaissance that will make all Americans proud of our Capital," bill sponsor Sen. Sam Brownback, R-Kansas, said at a "community meeting" convened to discuss the new bill.
Brownback chairs the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee's subpanel on D.C. Other sponsors of the bill are Sens. Connie Mack, R-Fla., and Joe Lieberman, D-Conn.

The bill circulated on Capitol Hill Friday as D.C. and U.S. Office of Management and Budget officials signed a "memorandum of understanding" that lays the groundwork for congressional debate over a multi-billion-dollar White House plan to revitalize the District.
Participating in Friday's White House signing of the MOU were OMB chief Franklin Raines, D.C. Mayor Marion Barry, and D.C. Council members Charlene Drew Jarvis and Linda Cropp.

The Senators' tax cut bill, meanwhile, would set a uniform tax rate of 15 percent in the District and is similar to a measure introduced in the House by D.C.'s delegate to Congress, Eleanor Holmes Norton.
Cuts would range from 79 percent for people earning $15,000 to $30,000 annually, to 34 percent for those with incomes at $200,000 or more, according to a bill summary.

People earning under $30,000 yearly would have an increased standard deduction and personal exemption. The deduction would increase from $6,550 to $15,000 for single filers; from $8,450 to $25,000 for single heads of households; and from $11,800 to $30,000 for married joint filers.
Mortgage interest and charitable deductions would remain unchanged, under the bill.

The senators' bill calls for a zero capital gains tax rate for D.C. residents on investments made within the city. Capital gains taxes also would be zeroed out for non-D.C. residents with investments in the city, other than residential holdings, the summary says.
The bill also would allow a $5,000 first-time D.C. credit for home buyers. A "brownfields" provision would permit immediate expensing of environmental clean up costs on new real estate purchases.
Norton's bill is identical except that it has no brownfields or first-time homebuyers provisions and there is no call for capital gains relief for non-D.C. residents.
Bill co-sponsor Mack said that, if enacted, the measure will kick off similar campaigns for tax reform nationwide.

"Once America sees what economic growth through a lower tax rate and zero capital gains tax rate can produce, the rest of the country will demand the same opportunity for more jobs, stronger investments, and greater hope for the future," Mack said.
